title: World's largest olive oil company plummets 20% after rivals agree to takeover deal
description: Bottles of Spanish olive oil are displayed for sale at a Carrefour supermarket in Spain.Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesShares of Deoleo, the
body: Bottles of Spanish olive oil are displayed for sale at a Carrefour supermarket in Spain.Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesShares of Deoleo, the world's largest olive oil company, plummeted Thursday after two rivals announced plans to acquire the company, a deal that would further consolidate Spain's dominance in the sector. Spanish olive oil firms Dcoop and Acesur will each hold a 50% stake in the company, resulting in a new olive oil giant in the region. The deal is intended to boost olive oil consumption worldwide and support farmers in creating value through the supply chain, Dcoop said in an announcement.Deoleo said in a separate statement that it has accepted the offer, which implies an enterprise value of 520 million euros ($583.2 million )."This milestone marks the start of a new phase, built on solid foundations and with a long-term vision to continue creating value for the sector and all our stakeholders," said Deoleo CEO Cristóbal Valdés. Deoleo was last trading down 19.9%. However, the stock is up around 55% since the beginning of the year as it's benefited from a moderation in olive oil prices that has helped lift U.S. sales. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconDeoleo shares since the beginning of the year. The news comes after an intensifying takeover battle between Dcoop and multinational firms including those from Italy, France, and Australia. The stock gained over 20% on Aug. 19 when news of the takeover battle emerged. Dcoop reportedly previously offered 470 million euros ($545 million) for Deoleo.Spain is one of the world's leading olive oil producers and is often used as a global reference for prices. Prices for the commodity have been volatile over the past few years as supplies swung dramatically one season to the next, with climate change, water scarcity, and pest and disease playing a role. Deoleo's Valdés told CNBC in July that the period between 2022 and 2024 was one of the most challenging periods for the sector, but that prices are now stabilizing due to favourable rain trends. "The highly complex market cycle experienced between 2022 and 2024, which had a severe yet temporary impact on the industry, is now definitively behind us," Valdés said at the time.

schema.headline: World's largest olive oil company plummets 20% after rivals agree to takeover deal

title: Barkin sees interest rate hikes ahead, but at a gradual pace
description: Richmond Federal Reserve President Thomas Barkin said Thursday that he expects the central bank will have to raise interest rates further, though he's
body: Richmond Federal Reserve President Thomas Barkin said Thursday that he expects the central bank will have to raise interest rates further, though he's not sure by how much or at what pace.In a CNBC interview that was part of the Richmond Fed's 2026 CFO Summit, the policymaker expressed concern over inflation and said monetary policy will need to adjust."Unemployment's near record lows, and inflation is too high. That means the path is pretty straightforward. The question, of course, is pace," Barkin said in the talk with CNBC's Steve Liesman."Gradual makes sense if you think there's uncertainty in the world, and if you think that there's information you're going to get in the period. And I think that's still a pace that makes sense to me," he added.Barkin's comments come a little more than a week after his colleagues voted to keep the Fed's benchmark overnight borrowing rate anchored in a range between 3.75% and 4%. While Barkin is not a voting member on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee now, he will be in 2027.In its post-meeting statement, the FOMC said that it is awaiting the "accumulation of more information" as it deliberates where to go next. When the committee OK'd a quarter percentage point hike in September, officials largely agreed that another increase was likely before the end of 2026.Markets are pricing in a better than 80% chance of a hike in December, then one more move in 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.Barkin said he considers current policy close to a point where it neither restricts nor promotes growth, which officials consider a neutral rate.Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond President Thomas Barkin attends a conversation with the Economic Club of Washington DC in Washington, D.C., U.S., April 9, 2025. Kevin Mohatt | Reuters"If you're restricting the economy, presumably you're restricting consumption, which is you know roughly two thirds of the economy, and that's relatively elevated," he said. "So that would make the case that we're a little bit accommodative."Inflation, he added, "is the most important risk right now ... and I hope that our move in September and whatever else we might choose to do in the future will have some impact on inflation."Artificial intelligence is one source of price pressures, though he said it eventually will spur production and help ease inflation farther down the road.In a related matter, he said the debt issuance to hyperscalers, estimated this year at better than $500 billion, is "worth watching" for potential credit issues."It's always it's pretty hard to convince yourself that some of these big hyperscalers who are generating so much cash from their core businesses aren't good credits," he said. "So it's more who are the intermediaries in this world who are taking on risks that you don't know about ... You do wonder where in the intermediary sector is the biggest risk."

schema.headline: Barkin sees interest rate hikes ahead, but at a gradual pace

title: Nintendo Switch 2 sales plunge 41% as price hikes and memory crunch bite
description: A Super Mario character is pictured at a Nintendo display ahead of the launch of the company's Switch 2 console, at an electronics store in Nagoya, Ja
body: A Super Mario character is pictured at a Nintendo display ahead of the launch of the company's Switch 2 console, at an electronics store in Nagoya, Japan, June 2, 2025.Richard A. Brooks | Afp | Getty ImagesSales of Nintendo's flagship Switch 2 plunged in its fiscal second quarter after the Japanese gaming giant rolled out price hikes amid soaring memory costs.Nintendo said it sold 2.67 million units of the Switch 2 in the three months ended Sept. 30, down 41% from the same period last year. That was also lower than the 3.82 million units sold in the prior quarter. During the quarter, Nintendo rolled out price increases for the Switch 2 in the U.S., Canada and Japan after hiking the cost of the device in Japan earlier in the year.Memory, a core component of Nintendo's consoles, continues to face a supply shortage and huge demand, which is driving an unprecedented price surge for the chips.  Still, the Japanese gaming giant stuck to its previous Switch 2 sales forecast of 16.5 million units in the current fiscal year, which ends in March 2027.Here's how Nintendo did in its fiscal second quarter, compared with LSEG average estimates:Revenue: 448.2 billion Japanese yen ($2.8 billion) versus 481.37 billion yen expectedNet profit: 73.5 billion yen versus 82.16 billion yenInvestors eye future releasesWhile the Kyoto-headquartered firm has had some strong games this year, including "Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream" and "Pokémon Pokopia", which became a surprise viral hit, there are no major marquee titles.Investors hope that "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time," a remake of one of Nintendo's most iconic games, could boost Switch 2 sales in the coming weeks. The game was released on Thursday. "Nintendo's only real blockbuster this fiscal year is the Ocarina Of Time remake. It's not enough to make investors happy, especially after the device is now as expensive as it is," Serkan Toto, CEO of Kantan Games, told CNBC."It's getting harder and harder to sell video game hardware these days, and only hits help. Nintendo must step on the gas and deliver more big games next fiscal year to make sure the Switch 2 momentum continues."Nintendo also has new Pokémon games slated for release in 2027.

schema.headline: Nintendo Switch 2 sales plunge 41% as price hikes and memory crunch bite

title: Rheinmetall shares plunge 17% after outlook cut as military contracts stall
description: German defense giant Rheinmetall cut its full-year guidance late Wednesday, citing delays to military contracts and ammunition deliveries.It marks the
body: German defense giant Rheinmetall cut its full-year guidance late Wednesday, citing delays to military contracts and ammunition deliveries.It marks the company's second outlook cut since August, when Germany scrapped plans to build warships in what would have been Rheinmetall's biggest order since World War II. The defense company now expects sales to rise to around 13.2 billion euros ($14.9 billion) in 2026, down from a prior outlook range of between 13.7 billion and 14.2 billion euros. It is expected to have an operating margin of around 18.5%, down from the previously expected 19%.Rheinmetall said it revised its 2026 guidance due to delays in the German military's Arminius project, a major German military procurement program for Boxer armored vehicles, and setbacks in artillery ammunition acceptance testing. The Arminius contract, now expected to be commissioned next year, involves vehicles manufactured by ARTEC, a joint venture between Rheinmetall and the Franco-German defense group KNDS.Rheinmetall shares fell over 17% in early trading, bringing year-to-date losses to about 46%.It follows an average annual gain of 119% over the prior four years as it became one of the main beneficiaries of ramped-up military spending by European governments amid Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconRheinmetall shares over the past five years.RBC analysts called the announcement "clearly negative," citing concerns over the Boxer program's timing, scope and impact on medium-term guidance. They warned the news could fuel broader investor concerns about traditional defense technology."We suspect bears will see this negatively as part of the ongoing 'new-tech vs old-tech' sector debate," they said.Rheinmetall said delays to the Boxer contract would also push expected advance payments into 2027, affecting its previous cash conversion target of over 40%, although it still expects positive operating free cash flow this year.The company also flagged delays in expected fourth-quarter revenue from new business activities, particularly its partnership with Dutch defense technology firm Destinus.The guidance cut came as the German company posted improving results, with third-quarter sales increasing 32% year-on-year to 3.15 billion euros and operating profit jumping 62% to 553 million euros.New order intake was 2.89 billion euros, bringing its backlog to 78 billion euros by the end of the third quarter.Despite being overshadowed by the outlook cut, Citi analysts called the third-quarter print "a strong set of Q3 results."

schema.headline: Rheinmetall shares plunge 17% after outlook cut as military contracts stall

title: E.l.f. Beauty posts 51% sales increase, raises full-year guidance
description: e.l.f Cosmetics e.l.f CosmeticsE.l.f. Beauty on Wednesday blew past Wall Street expectations as it posted a 51% increase in net sales in its second fi
body: e.l.f Cosmetics e.l.f CosmeticsE.l.f. Beauty on Wednesday blew past Wall Street expectations as it posted a 51% increase in net sales in its second fiscal quarter.The beauty company said it saw its 31st consecutive quarter of net sales growth, attributing the streak to strong performance across its portfolio. The revenue spike was driven by both retail and e-commerce channels across the U.S. and internationally, the company added."The thing I'm most pleased about is we saw strength across our entire portfolio," CEO Tarang Amin told CNBC in an interview. "Every one of our brands contributed strong growth this quarter."Amin added that E.l.f. is the most-searched brand on TikTok Shop and the No. 2 brand in cosmetics on the platform. The company also said it saw strong results for Rhode, the skincare brand it acquired last year. The company raised its full fiscal-year guidance following the better-than-anticipated quarter. It now expects net sales in the range of $2 billion to $2.03 billion, compared with a previous range of between $1.94 billion and $1.97 billion. It also upped its adjusted EBITDA projection to a range of $421 million to $427 million from between $401 million and $407 million.E.l.f. said it now expects adjusted earnings per share for the year to come in between $3.82 and $3.86, exceeding prior guidance of between $3.50 and $3.55 per share. It's also expecting a net income range of $231 million to $233 million, up from a previous range of $212 million to $215 million.It had already raised its guidance last quarter after outperforming its expectations.Amin said the company is "very bullish" on the holiday season, expecting high sales through the end of the year. Here's how the company performed in its second fiscal quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: $1.21 adjusted vs. 60 cents expectedRevenue: $520.8 million vs. $470.3 millionFor the period ended Sept. 30, E.l.f. reported net income of $30.03 million, or 50 cents per share, up significantly from roughly $3 million, or 5 cents per share, the year prior.Net sales grew 51% to $520.8 million. E.l.f. also saw significant growth in its international channels, with business up 165%. Amin told CNBC that only 25% of the company's business is outside of the U.S. and that it has a "tremendous opportunity" to build on that momentum.The company also said its gross margin increased 1.6% during the quarter, including a 0.3% benefit from tariff refunds. Amin previously said the retailer planned to fully reinvest that money into pricing and marketing to continue driving growth.Though E.l.f. received most of its refunds in its first fiscal quarter, some of those funds flowed through the second quarter, and the company expects to receive a yearly total of around $55 million. Amin told CNBC on Wednesday that the company lowered the price of about 10% of its units by $1 because of the tariff benefits."We're seeing great unit momentum based on that," he said.

schema.headline: E.l.f. Beauty posts 51% sales increase, raises full-year guidance

title: Expedia CEO says AI agents aren't changing booking habits — yet
description: watch nowExpedia CEO Ariane Gorin said Thursday the company hasn't yet seen artificial intelligence agents affecting the way customers book, but the e
body: watch nowExpedia CEO Ariane Gorin said Thursday the company hasn't yet seen artificial intelligence agents affecting the way customers book, but the early signs show potential for an industry shift. "It's a great way for people to do inspiration, to do trip planning," Gorin said in an interview with CNBC. "We haven't seen it change the way they're actually doing booking." The comments come as personal AI agents like Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots enter the mainstream, promising to tackle everything from scheduling to shopping for everyday Americans. Opportunities in travel planning and booking could pose a competitive threat to traditional sites like Expedia. Gorin said Expedia is "working with all of the agents" to make sure it surfaces in AI results, to understand how the agents get information and to make sure that the company has the necessary integrations. She acknowledged it's possible that AI agents could develop their own travel programs and eventually claim market share, but she said complexities within the industry — customer service, for example — would be difficult to fully replace with artificial intelligence. "People were already shopping across a number of places, so the agent can do that in a much easier way," Gorin said. "But when it comes to actually booking — being confident that the content that you're getting is right, the amenities are right, the price is right, if something goes wrong, someone's going to actually either solve it for you, answer the phone, be there for you — I don't think those agents are going to do it for you, and that's why people trust Expedia and come to us."Shares of Expedia were down about 12% Thursday after the company delivered weaker-than-expected guidance for the fourth quarter on Wednesday. The company forecast revenue of between $3.69 billion and $3.75 billion for the final three months of the year, making the midpoint lower than analyst estimates of $3.74 billion, according to FactSet. Gorin attributed the "moderation" in Expedia's fourth-quarter guidance to "geopolitical events in the Middle East and Europe," the midterm elections and the company moving its fall sale from the fourth quarter to the third quarter. But she noted the company reported a strong third quarter, as total gross bookings rose 11% and revenue climbed 12%.

schema.headline: Expedia CEO says AI agents aren't changing booking habits — yet

title: LIV Golf faces liquidation after BC Partners scraps rescue plan
description: A general view of the 18th hole during day four of LIV Golf Indianapolis at The Club at Chatham Hills on Aug. 23, 2026 in Westfield, Indiana. Michael
body: A general view of the 18th hole during day four of LIV Golf Indianapolis at The Club at Chatham Hills on Aug. 23, 2026 in Westfield, Indiana. Michael Miller | ISI Photos | Getty ImagesLIV Golf could be headed for liquidation after BC Partners Credit reportedly dropped plans to finance a relaunch of the breakaway league.The investment firm had pledged up to $300 million for a revamped version of LIV, known as LIV 2.0, but withdrew the plan after LIV Golf failed to secure enough player commitments, according to the Associated Press.LIV is scheduled to appear in U.S. bankruptcy court Thursday, with the hearing now expected to focus on liquidation of its assets. The league's ultimate fate remains unclear.LIV Golf and BC Partners did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.LIV filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund said it would stop funding the league after the 2026 season.PIF had invested more than $5 billion since LIV launched in 2022, according to its Chapter 11 filing.BC Partners' proposed relaunch would have made players majority owners of the reorganized league and featured a scaled-back schedule. But LIV has lost several prominent players, including Jon Rahm and Sergio Garcia, as it sought commitments for the new venture.Rahm said Tuesday that uncertainty over the league's future and proposed changes to its format influenced his decision to leave."There were too many unknowns at the time, and there's still quite a few," he told reporters ahead of the Abu Dhabi Championship. Rahm added that the revamped competition appeared to be moving away from the team format that initially attracted him.Garcia, who secured a release from his LIV contract in October, has outlined plans to return to the DP World Tour and explore a possible return to the PGA Tour.Only four players had publicly committed to LIV 2.0: Richard Bland, Cameron Tringale, Brendan Steele and Ben Campbell, according to Golf Digest.LIV launched in 2022 as a challenger to the PGA Tour, recruiting prominent players including Phil Mickelson, Dustin Johnson and Bryson DeChambeau with lucrative contracts.Its arrival split men's professional golf, with the PGA Tour suspending members who competed in LIV events. The disputes later spilled into the courts, with players challenging suspensions and the rival organizations pursuing competing legal claims.The PGA Tour denied the allegations, while LIV dismissed the counterclaims.A June 2023 framework agreement between the PGA Tour, DP World Tour and PIF ended their litigation and proposed combining their commercial businesses, although the deal was never completed.

schema.headline: LIV Golf faces liquidation after BC Partners scraps rescue plan

title: Consumers are spending on physical gifts even as travel tops wish lists, Visa survey finds
description: A shopper browses shoes at a Skechers store in San Francisco, California, June 10, 2026. U.S inflation accelerated in May to the fastest pace in more
body: A shopper browses shoes at a Skechers store in San Francisco, California, June 10, 2026. U.S inflation accelerated in May to the fastest pace in more than three years as the Iran war pushed up energy prices, outstripping Americans' pay gains.Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesConsumers are hoping for more travel and experiences this holiday season, but physical gifts continue to win the lion's share of their wallets, according to a new report from Visa on Thursday.The report found that more than half of survey respondents are putting travel and live events at the top of their wish lists. Still, only 15% of those respondents are prioritizing spending on experiences for others, while 27% of them plan to favor physical gifts.That gap between what shoppers want and what they plan to buy is largely due to higher travel costs, lower consumer sentiment and an emphasis on value, according to Michael Brown, Visa's principal U.S. economist."There is some interesting trade-offs there that we're seeing on the part of consumers," Brown told CNBC. "If I'm traveling more, I'm probably going to be gifting those physical goods less, so this is really the broader context."The survey was conducted among roughly 4,660 U.S. adults ages 18 and older, designed to be representative of the broader population of consumers.Brown said budget pressure also factors into traveling for the holidays, as Visa expects more people to celebrate the holidays "a little bit closer to home" than in the past given rising airfares and general inflation. In September, consumer prices rose 3.7% annually, driven higher by surging energy costs.Airlines have hiked the price of plane tickets this year as their fuel costs have risen by billions of dollars due to the war in the Middle East. And even if fuel prices drop, executives have said fares are likely to stay high, with fares up more than 22% in September compared with a year earlier, according to the consumer price index. Those trends mean consumers will likely be more intentional about where they're spending, especially as inflation drives up prices across the board."Consumers are aspirational. They want those experiences, they want to travel, they want to be out in the world," Brown said. "However, the economic reality is with prices rising, with economic uncertainty, they need to balance the reality of today's economic environment with those aspirations."The report also found that only households with an income above $200,000 spent more on trips departing between Nov. 1 and early next year compared with 2025 into 2026. On the other hand, many other income groups pulled back on their travel spending. "If you think about that segment, a lot of them own equities, and the equity market runup over the last several months has created a lot of positivity among that specific affluent demographic, and I think that's one of the factors that continues to motivate even aggregate macro spend today," Brown said.Meanwhile, less affluent shoppers are placing an emphasis on value. Visa's consumer survey from October showed that roughly one-third of consumers with an income below $100,000 are going to switch to lower-cost brands or stores when shopping for holiday gifts this season. Though Visa is projecting a 4.5% year-over-year increase in holiday sales growth, much of that figure is due to inflation. Without those price increases, sales are expected to rise just 1.1% this year, down from the 1.3% increase during the 2025 holiday season.Ultimately, Brown said the survey findings may be encouraging for the broader retail scene this holiday season. With less emphasis on travel and more projected spending on physical gifts, it could boost the sector at a time when spending is under pressure. At the same time, he said that consumers may just be expecting to spend more this holiday season because they've become accustomed to the higher prices. "But, of course, consumers are internalizing higher prices of things, and I think that's why they're reporting higher anticipated spend this year," Brown said. "I think these numbers just need to be looked at through the lens of the inflation and particularly consumers' perception of where inflation is going to go. I think that weighed heavily on consumer psychology this season."

schema.headline: Consumers are spending on physical gifts even as travel tops wish lists, Visa survey finds

title: Democrats to probe JPMorgan's relationship with Epstein when they take Senate control
description: Senator Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon, during a news conference at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, June 17, 2026. Daniel Heuer
body: Senator Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon, during a news conference at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, June 17, 2026. Daniel Heuer | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesSenate Democrats are gearing up to investigate JPMorgan Chase's banking relationship with disgraced sex offender Jeffrey Epstein once they take control of Congress early next year.Democratic staffers on the Senate Finance Committee, which is likely to be chaired in the next Congress by Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., intend to home in on how high-ranking executives at the nation's largest bank handled Epstein, a source familiar with the committee's thinking told CNBC on Thursday. The person spoke on condition of anonymity because the probe has not been announced.They aim to focus in particular on the Epstein-related decisions made by Mary Erdoes, CEO of the bank's Asset & Wealth Management business, according to the source.JPMorgan did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.Democrats are openly preparing to put a spotlight back on Epstein as they plan to launch sweeping investigations following their wipeout victories in Tuesday's midterm elections.Wyden, who is currently the committee's ranking member, has made clear he plans to make full use of the subpoena powers that committee majorities wield.This is developing news. Please check back for updates.

schema.headline: Democrats to probe JPMorgan's relationship with Epstein when they take Senate control

title: Banks are turning cautious on lending, according to the Fed. What it means for the economy
description: U.S. banks are starting to tighten their lending standards amid growing concern over the underlying health of the economy, according to a new Federal
body: U.S. banks are starting to tighten their lending standards amid growing concern over the underlying health of the economy, according to a new Federal Reserve survey.The Fed's latest Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey on Bank Lending Practices for October, published Nov. 2, showed an uneven credit backdrop in the third quarter, with smaller businesses, riskier households and commercial property in particular facing a lending squeeze.The latest quarterly SLOOS study for October — which pulled together responses from 61 domestic banks and 18 U.S. branches of foreign lenders — covered changes in lending standards, terms and demand during the third quarter.The survey tracks banks' reported lending standards, terms and demand, not actual loan volumes, offering a snapshot of evolving credit conditions and sentiment.Small businesses feel the squeezeCommercial and industrial lending to large and middle-market firms was broadly unchanged from the previous survey — but banks tightened lending to smaller businesses."Banks reported tightening standards for premiums charged on riskier loans for firms of all sizes," the report noted. Lenders pointed to a less favorable or more uncertain economic outlook, and a worsening of industry-specific problems as the key reason for the shift.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconU.S. 10-Year Treasurys.Commercial real estate is also emerging as a pressure point, with banks reporting tightened standards across the board on construction and land development, nonfarm nonresidential properties, and multifamily properties, and weakening demand for loans in all CRE categories. U.S. banks are also tightening credit standards for nonbank financial firms such as private equity funds and business and mortgage credit intermediaries. The pullback comes amid growing demand for liquidity from private equity funds and business credit intermediaries, with lenders again highlighting prevailing economic uncertainty and concerns over the deteriorating financial strength among NDFI borrowers.Household credit turns selectiveMeanwhile, household credit sentiment appears mixed. While banks have left mortgage standards broadly unchanged, there has been some easing for jumbo mortgages — but tighter rules for subprime loans — as banks reported weaker demand, on balance, across all residential real estate loan categories."Banks reported being more likely to approve credit card applications to super-prime and prime borrowers and less likely to approve applications to subprime borrowers, with small banks driving the trend for subprime borrowers," the report added. watch nowThe squeeze comes as borrowing costs moved sharply higher during the third quarter. The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — hit an intraday high of 5.349% on Oct. 5, its highest level since April 2002, amid concerns over rising U.S. debt.Tiffany Wilding, managing director and economist at PIMCO, said small businesses, housing and debt-laden firms face tighter credit and higher borrowing costs as the AI investment boom squeezes other parts of the U.S. economy.  "Higher government bond yields have catalyzed a broader repricing of credit risk, especially for lower-quality borrowers," Wilding said in a note Oct. 28.Signals of credit stress among riskier households chime with a recent CNBC and SurveyMonkey poll, which found that one in five Americans who rent or have a mortgage spend at least half of their pretax income on housing, while 49% spend between 25% and 49%. Lender guidance recommends consumers spend 28% to 30% of their income on housing.A separate Federal Reserve report indicated that U.S. families' ability to address their debts has worsened over the past three years. The Fed's latest Survey of Consumer Finances, released Oct. 9, found that the percentage of families behind on loan payments at the end of 2025 reached almost 20%, up from about 12% in the previous survey in 2022.

schema.headline: Banks are turning cautious on lending, according to the Fed. What it means for the economy

title: Democrats flip dozens of GOP seats. Republicans haven't flipped a single one
description: The U.S. Capitol is seen in Washington on Nov. 4, 2026, a day after midterm elections in which Democrats secured control of both the House of Represen
body: The U.S. Capitol is seen in Washington on Nov. 4, 2026, a day after midterm elections in which Democrats secured control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, shifting the balance of power in Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term.Mehmet Eser | Anadolu | Getty ImagesSeven Senate seats. At least 24 House districts. Five governorships. Twelve state legislative chambers. By Wednesday afternoon, that's how far Democrats' historic midterm rout had reached.Republicans, meanwhile, had yet to flip a single Democratic-held congressional seat, governorship or state legislative chamber, according to Associated Press data. Their remaining opportunities for congressional pickups are largely confined to two newly gerrymandered House districts that weren't even supposed to be competitive in the first place.The lopsided results underscored the breadth of the GOP's shellacking, with Democrats breaking decades of Republican dominance in reliably red states and reshaping the balance of power from Washington to state capitols.As of late Wednesday, nine House seats remained uncalled by the AP along with two Senate seats and two governors races. The one seat Republicans may have a chance of flipping that hasn't been redistricted ahead of this election is Maine's 2nd District, FiftyPlusOne head of research Mary Radcliffe said by email.In Kansas, voters elected their first Democratic U.S. senator since 1932, ending a 94-year losing streak for the party. In Texas, Democrats toppled three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott and captured a Senate seat that had eluded the party since 1988. Republican-held Senate seats also fell in Iowa, South Carolina and Ohio, along with seats in Maine and North Carolina.The same wave swept through governors' mansions. Democrats scored upsets in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Nevada — all states President Donald Trump won in 2024 — giving the party a majority of the nation's governorships for the first time since 2010.Upheaval even reached state capitols, where Republican legislative majorities that had endured for decades fell like dominoes.Democrats seized control of the Texas House for the first time in more than two decades, flipped both chambers of the Wisconsin Legislature and wrested the North Carolina House from Republicans after 16 years in the minority.In Pennsylvania, Democrats captured the state Senate for the first time since before 1994, giving the party complete control of state government. They also reclaimed lower chambers in Michigan and Minnesota, restoring full Democratic control in both states. In Arizona, unofficial results pointed toward Democrats taking both legislative chambers for the first time in roughly 60 years.Even where Republicans held on to legislative majorities, Democrats stripped away veto-proof supermajorities in Florida, Indiana, Kansas and Missouri. Not since the aftermath of Watergate in 1974 had the GOP faced a statehouse reckoning of this magnitude, according to the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee.The scale of the losses is all the more remarkable given how aggressively Republicans had tried to protect their power. At Trump's urging, GOP lawmakers spent months pursuing an extraordinary mid-decade redistricting campaign, redrawing congressional boundaries in Texas, Florida and North Carolina to tilt the electoral map in their favor.Yet the gerrymandering push did little to blunt the Democratic wave. And the damage might not be over. Republicans were still fighting to hold Senate seats in Alaska and Mississippi, with several House contests also yet to be called Wednesday.— Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Democrats flip dozens of GOP seats. Republicans haven't flipped a single one

title: Bomb threats disrupt flights across Europe for the second time. Here’s what we know
description: A LOT Polish Airlines passenger aircraft takes off from the runway at Brussels Airport following security checks after making an emergency landing due
body: A LOT Polish Airlines passenger aircraft takes off from the runway at Brussels Airport following security checks after making an emergency landing due to a bomb threat, in Brussels, Belgium, on November 5, 2026. Anadolu | Anadolu | Getty ImagesFlights across Europe were targeted by "hoax" bomb threats on Thursday for the second time this week, disrupting air travel across London, Dublin, and Helsinki, among others. At least 27 different flights were impacted, according to Reuters, with some forced to land unexpectedly and others escorted by fighter jets. Aer Lingus, Finnair, Wizz Air and Polish airline LOT confirmed to CNBC that some of their flights were affected. It comes after seven passenger planes across Europe, two departing from the U.K., were targeted by suspected bomb threats on Tuesday and were described as "malicious hoax threats" by the U.K. government. Finnair said two of its flights — one from Helsinki to Rome with 144 passengers and 7 crew members and another from Helsinki to Vienna with 177 passengers and six crew members — received "unfounded or hoax" bomb threats on Thursday, with both flights landing safely and customers disembarking the aircraft. Here's what we know so farLocal authorities in Rome and Vienna inspected the two flights and didn't find anything out of the ordinary. "Unfortunately, air traffic is sometimes subject to threats, as we have seen this week, when other airlines in Europe have also faced hoax bomb threats," Finnair said in a statement. "Threats are almost always unfounded." Hungarian budget carrier Wizz Air confirmed to CNBC that its flight from Milan's Malpensa Airport to Bucharest's Otopeni Airport, as well as another flight to Warsaw, were subject to bomb threats on Thursday. The flight to Bucharest was approaching its final destination and landed safely when the threat was reported at Otopeni, with security checks subsequently clearing the aircraft. Wizz Air's Warsaw flight was diverted. "This incident comes amid a series of similar bomb threats affecting several airlines across Europe in recent days," Wizz Air told CNBC. "Wizz Air is not the only airline targeted, with other carriers also experiencing threats resulting in flight diversions and security checks."Irish airline Aer Lingus diverted its Dublin to Rome flight to Normandy on Thursday morning, while Polish airline LOT said two of its flights from Warsaw received security threats. Both were cleared following security inspections, the airlines told CNBC. Air France's CEO Ben Smith said none of its flights were affected, but the coordinated threats are unprecedented. "It's unfortunate, and we hope it won't give consumers any reason to slow down or reduce their travel plans."U.S. Transport Secretary Sean Duffy told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Thursday that the incidents appeared to be "false attacks." He added: "We take safety very seriously, which is why, if you see any issue in the airspace or threats in the airspace, we shut it down...and so, with all of our assets in the U.S. government and our partners over in Europe, we are tracking this together and working together to make sure the American airspace, the American traveler, is safe."European Union Commissioner for Sustainable Transport and Tourism, Apostolos Tzitzikostas cautioned it is "too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked," in a post on X. "The EU-level information-sharing mechanism has been activated related to aviation security."

schema.headline: Bomb threats disrupt flights across Europe for the second time. Here’s what we know

title: What the Democratic midterms sweep changes for U.S.-China relations
description: U.S. President Donald Trump (R) greets President of China Xi Jinping as he arrives to the South Portico of the White House on September 25, 2026 in Wa
body: U.S. President Donald Trump (R) greets President of China Xi Jinping as he arrives to the South Portico of the White House on September 25, 2026 in Washington, DC. Andrew Harnik | Getty ImagesBEIJING — Democrats taking power from Republicans in Congress raises risks for U.S.-China tensions around Taiwan, while hardening tech competition, analysts said.The Democrats swept this week's midterm elections, taking majorities in the House and Senate and flipping governors' offices in places like Texas, Nevada and Iowa. Most of the new election winners, however, won't begin their terms until January.Before then, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping will likely maintain their fragile truce by meeting twice: in Shenzhen this month, and in Miami, Florida, next month."As a lame duck who is increasingly focused on his personal legacy rather than the Republican Party's success, Trump may resist increased pressure for confrontation with China and continue his pursuit of 'strategic stability,'" Gabriel Wildau, managing director at Teneo, said in an email.High on the Democrats' agenda is removing Trump's tariffs, as part of a broader focus on addressing domestic inflation, CNBC has learned."On balance as a result of the midterms the Democrats may nudge the U.S.'s China policy in a more hawkish direction through hearings and legislation, particularly on economic security issues and Taiwan," said Scott Kennedy, senior advisor and trustee chair in Chinese business and economics at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.But any efforts will "be constrained by the executive branch's wide range of latitude and China's growing power and leverage, which can't be easily undone," he said.Beijing has hosted a flurry of global leaders this year, while major economies have struggled to slow a surge of imports from China. Chinese dominance in rare earths has given Beijing leverage in trade talks with the U.S. and the EU.Taiwan"Taiwan remains the most dangerous issue in U.S.-China relations and, in my view, the area where a Democratic Congress is most likely to challenge Beijing," wrote George Chen, partner and co-chair of digital practice at consultancy The Asia Group."Congress has repeatedly shown a willingness to pursue Taiwan initiatives even when administrations are more cautious," he said, noting Trump's balancing act will likely become more difficult.Nancy Pelosi's visit to Taiwan while House Speaker in 2022 angered Beijing, which considers the democratically self-governed island part of its territory. The U.S. maintains unofficial relations with Taiwan under a "One China" policy.Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is poised to become the first Black Speaker of the House in U.S. history, met in 2023 in New York with Tsai Ing-wen, who was then president of Taiwan.During Trump's trip to Beijing in May, Xi warned that mishandling Taiwan would put U.S.-China relations in "great jeopardy."Maintaining stability over Taiwan has grown more critical in the artificial intelligence race as the island is home to semiconductor giant TSMC, which manufactures many of Nvidia's chips.Over the last several years, the U.S. government has tightened restrictions on the ability of Chinese companies to buy advanced chips from Nvidia, spurring Beijing's efforts to develop its own version of the technology.Tech competitionU.S. stocks surged Wednesday after Trump accepted the Democrats' election wins, and oil prices fell following indications Washington would do more to end the Iran war. Apple and most "Magnificent Seven" tech stocks surged, despite declines in Nvidia.But there's an "emergence of a broader consensus in Washington that America's technological lead should not be used to strengthen China's military or strategic capabilities," Chen said, noting a Democratic Congress may be motivated to be more aggressive."As a result, Beijing may discover that technology becomes a growing source of friction even if Trump and Xi continue to maintain relatively cordial summit diplomacy," he said. The tech outlook ultimately depends on bigger questions about AI.Chinese tech stocks climbed Thursday, extending a recent rebound from a sharp sell-off last month. Beijing's latest regulatory intervention has helped support the market, said WisdomTree's Liqian Ren. But she said Chinese tech stock performance is ultimately tied more to global investor sentiment on AI."There's a lot of uncertainty on how much AI can deliver for U.S., or for China," she said. —CNBC's Justin Papp and Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

title: Chinese AI lab Moonshot turned to Europe for Nvidia Blackwell access amid U.S. China curbs, sources tell CNBC
description: Moonshot AI, a Chinese artificial intelligence lab that the White House accused of accessing Nvidia advanced chips remotely in East Asia, has sought a
body: Moonshot AI, a Chinese artificial intelligence lab that the White House accused of accessing Nvidia advanced chips remotely in East Asia, has sought access to the chips through data centers in Europe, sources have told CNBC.Deals have been discussed this year for Moonshot to rent capacity from neoclouds hosting Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, at facilities in Europe, four people familiar with the matter said. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.Nvidia's effective monopoly over the most powerful chips has made U.S. export controls a key tool in Washington's effort to preserve its advantage over China in the AI race. American AI labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic are locked in a training and pricing battle with Chinese developers, including Moonshot AI, which makes the Kimi family of models.Moonshot was looking to lease capacity powered by Nvidia's Blackwell systems, advanced chips currently subject to those export controls which effectively ban their import into China, three of the sources told CNBC.In July, the White House said the Chinese AI lab had accessed Nvidia's Blackwell chips via a facility in Thailand.U.S. export controls restrict the shipment of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China, but remote access via overseas data centers offers a loophole. Current law does not give regulators broad authority to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.Moonshot, Nvidia, the White House, the U.S. Department of Commerce, China's embassy in the U.K. and its Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not respond to a request for comment.Chinese developers have made notable capability gains in the past six months and greater access to Nvidia chips could put even more pressure on their American rivals.JINAN, CHINA - JULY 17: In this photo illustration, the logo of Kimi K3 is displayed on a smartphone screen on July 17, 2026 in Jinan, Shandong Province of China. (Photo by VCG/VCG via Getty Images)Vcg | Visual China Group | Getty ImagesTo lease Nvidia computing power in Europe, a Chinese AI company would typically rent capacity from a non-Chinese neocloud or data center operator that can purchase advanced chips. Moonshot was interested in leasing capacity on clusters for inference, which refers to serving models to end users, in Europe, two of the sources said. One of the sources said they were also aware of interest in clusters for training.Talks for arrangements that would see Moonshot rent access to clusters of 8,000 or more Blackwell GPUs hosted in the region have taken place, one source said. They described the Chinese AI lab as "very aggressive" in its pursuit of more computing power.One of the sources told CNBC that talks on securing Moonshot compute in Europe had taken place since the White House said it had done so via Thailand. Moonshot did not comment at the time.Racing to secure computing powerFounded in 2023, Beijing-based Moonshot AI is one of China's leading model builders. It released a new model in July that Moonshot said closed the gap with leading systems built by Anthropic and OpenAI. The model saw significant uptake as a cheaper alternative to U.S. offerings. Chinese AI models have surged in global adoption in 2026, amid capability gains and lower costs than U.S. rivals.Around the time Kimi K3 was released, Moonshot said demand had stretched its capacity, and it temporarily paused new subscriptions to prioritize compute for current members. "We're adding capacity as fast as we can and will reopen new subscription spots in batches," the company said in a LinkedIn post. Leasing AI compute is a booming industry, with customers, or offtakers, typically taking capacity for a fee and paying an upfront cost to secure the deal, which is a percentage of the lifetime contract value.One source said it had been proposed that Moonshot pay 30% to 50% more upfront than a non-Chinese offtaker would.Arrangements with Chinese customers can be more lucrative upfront, as neoclouds and financing firms look to hedge against a potential future ban of remote access agreements. Political pressureIn Washington, lawmakers have proposed the Remote Access Security Act (RASA) to expand U.S. export controls to include the cloud-based access of critical hardware and software. It passed the House of Representatives in January but has not passed the Senate.watch nowThe Financial Times reported on Tuesday that the chip giant told cloud providers selling access to their chips that they must sell at least 51% of services to non-Chinese customers.Asked about the reports earlier this week, an Nvidia spokesperson said: "America cannot win the AI race unless America's AI infrastructure wins worldwide — if the world's clouds rely on foreign-made chips, the model and application layers will be foreign-built as well."Nvidia said in August that Washington had licensed some sales of its H200 AI chips, an older generation, but that "such sales were restricted" by the Chinese government, which has sought to boost domestic chipmakers by limiting access to Nvidia chips.

title: OpenAI pledges to halt NDAs in new data center policy proposal after election rebuke
description: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaking at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas on Oct. 27, 2026.CNBCOpenAI reaffirmed its promise to pay the full cost of powering dat
body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaking at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas on Oct. 27, 2026.CNBCOpenAI reaffirmed its promise to pay the full cost of powering data centers as part of a series of commitments the company published Thursday, two days after voters at the polls roundly rejected the rapid expansion of AI.The artificial intelligence company said in its commitments that for data centers it owns and operates, it will solicit community input, publish construction plans and stay away from using non-disclosure agreements with public officials. Additionally, in a policy blueprint, OpenAI encouraged policymakers to enact similar commitments as laws. "What we're doing with this blueprint is really laying out the best lessons that we have learned and committing to applying them as they go forward," OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane told reporters during a Wednesday briefing. "This will help ensure that there is a very high floor in terms of how people move forward."Other tech companies, including Meta, Microsoft, Google and Anthropic, have outlined several similar commitments.On Tuesday, Americans issued a stinging rebuke of data centers at the polls. Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures for all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday.Read more CNBC tech newsOpenAI pledges to halt NDAs in new data center policy proposal after election rebukeVoters rejected AI data centers over resource concerns. Here's why measuring water usage is hardNintendo Switch 2 sales plunge 41% as price hikes and memory crunch biteHyperscalers and Apple surge after election results remove investor uncertaintyOpposition to AI data centers mounted swiftly over the summer across both sides of the political aisle. Consumers grappling with inflation, rising grocery prices and stubbornly high prices at the pump grew worried that the facilities could exacerbate environmental harms, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss. For many, they became a physical manifestation of the widespread antipathy and anxiety around AI.AI companies like OpenAI depend on AI data centers to serve customers and develop new models, and they're seeking to build out as rapidly as possible to meet demand. In February, OpenAI told investors that it's targeting $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030, and the company has since announced massive data center projects in Georgia and Ohio. OpenAI has repeatedly pledged to protect ratepayers and invest in local communities this year, and Lehane said the company's latest commitments build on many of its previous initiatives. He said the policy blueprint has been in the works since August, and that he met with dozens of lawmakers and candidates since then."Having these conversations now actually helps put more energy into the momentum, so that when people come back in late January, new Congress is in in session, a lot of the work is being done in advance," Lehane said.
